title: Electrostatics and circuits
tagline: Charge, field, potential and steady currents
summary: Coulomb’s law, the electric field and Gauss’s law, electric potential, capacitors, current, resistance and direct-current circuits.
overview: Electricity begins with one new property of matter, charge, and one new field, the electric field, which tells a test charge what force it would feel. Everything else in this course — potential, capacitance, current, resistance — is built from that field together with the mechanics you already know. The field is the object; the force on a particular charge is an application.

Coulomb’s law and the superposition principle give the field of any static arrangement of charges, and Gauss’s law is the same statement rewritten so that symmetry does the integration. Potential turns a vector problem back into a scalar one. Capacitors store energy in the field. The last two chapters let the charges move slowly: current is a flux of charge, Ohm’s law is a material relation, and Kirchhoff’s rules are charge conservation and the loop rule for a conservative field.

Gauss’s law is easy to state and easy to misapply. It is always true; it is useful for computing a field only when symmetry makes the flux integral trivial. A conductor in electrostatics is an equipotential with no field in its interior, and that fact solves more problems than a direct integration does.
outcomes: Compute forces and fields of point charges by superposition, in Cartesian and polar language.
Use Gauss’s law for spherical, cylindrical and planar symmetry, and say why it does not help without symmetry.
Compute potential and potential difference, and recover the field as minus the gradient.
Find capacitance and stored energy for simple geometries and for combinations of capacitors.
Apply Ohm’s law, resistivity and the microscopic picture of drift velocity.
Analyse direct-current circuits with Kirchhoff’s rules, including RC transients.

history.title: Coulomb’s torsion balance
history.detail: Charles-Augustin de Coulomb measured the force between charged spheres with a torsion balance and found the inverse-square law that now carries his name.

history.title: Poisson’s equation
history.detail: Siméon Denis Poisson formulated the equation ∇²V = −ρ/ε₀ relating the electrostatic potential to the charge density.

history.title: Gauss’s flux law
history.detail: Gauss wrote the flux law for the electric field in 1835. It was published only in 1867, in his collected works.

history.title: Ohm’s law
history.detail: Georg Simon Ohm’s Die galvanische Kette stated that the current in a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it.

history.title: Kirchhoff’s rules
history.detail: As a student, Gustav Kirchhoff published the junction and loop rules that reduce a resistive network to linear equations.

history.title: Faraday and the dielectric
history.detail: Faraday found that filling a capacitor with an insulator increases its capacitance, the first evidence that the field in matter is not the field in vacuum.
